tests.title: Practice Test 1: Everyday Science
tests.passage:
Most people have had the experience of buying a fresh loaf of bread, only to find a few days later that it has become hard and dry. Many believe that bread goes stale simply because it loses water to the air. Scientists, however, have shown that the real reason is more surprising. In fact, a stale loaf may contain almost the same amount of water as a fresh one.

Bread is made mainly from flour, and flour contains a lot of starch. Starch is made of long chains of sugar molecules that are packed tightly together in tiny grains. When dough is baked in a hot oven, water enters these grains and the chains spread out. This process, known as gelatinisation, gives fresh bread its soft and springy texture.

As soon as the bread leaves the oven and begins to cool, the starch chains slowly start to move back together. They form a tight, ordered structure again and push water out of the grains. This change is called retrogradation. The water does not necessarily leave the loaf; much of it moves into the crust, which is why the crust of an old loaf often feels soft and leathery rather than crisp. Meanwhile, the inside of the loaf, which bakers call the crumb, becomes firm and crumbly.

Temperature has a strong effect on how fast this happens. Many people keep bread in the refrigerator, believing that the cold will keep it fresh for longer. Research suggests the opposite. At refrigerator temperatures, starch chains rejoin up to three times faster than at room temperature, so bread kept in the fridge goes stale much more quickly. Freezing, on the other hand, stops the process almost completely, because the water inside the bread turns to ice and the chains can no longer move. For this reason, bakers recommend freezing any bread that will not be eaten within two days.

Fortunately, staling can be partly reversed. If a stale loaf is heated in an oven to around 60 degrees Celsius or higher, the starch chains spread apart once more and the bread becomes soft again. However, this effect lasts only for a short time. Once the bread cools down, it goes stale even faster than before, so reheated bread should be eaten immediately.

Some types of bread stay fresh longer than others. Bread made with fat, such as butter or oil, tends to stay soft for more days, because the fat gets between the starch chains and slows down retrogradation. Sugar and certain natural ingredients added by bakers have a similar effect. Large loaves also go stale more slowly than small rolls, since they have less surface compared with their size.

Understanding staling is important for the food industry. Every year, a large amount of bread is thrown away in homes and shops, and much of it is wasted only because it has become hard, not because it is unsafe to eat. Food scientists hope that better knowledge of starch will help to reduce this waste. Until then, the best advice for consumers is simple: keep bread at room temperature in a closed bag if it will be eaten soon, and put the rest in the freezer.

questions.prompt: A stale loaf usually contains much less water than a fresh loaf.
questions.promptGu: વાસી બ્રેડમાં સામાન્ય રીતે તાજી બ્રેડ કરતાં ઘણું ઓછું પાણી હોય છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says: 'a stale loaf may contain almost the same amount of water as a fresh one'. 'Almost the same' is the opposite of 'much less', so the statement is FALSE.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 1 માં લખ્યું છે કે વાસી બ્રેડમાં તાજી બ્રેડ જેટલું જ લગભગ પાણી હોય છે ('almost the same amount'). પ્રશ્ન 'ઘણું ઓછું' કહે છે, જે ઊલટું છે. તેથી જવાબ FALSE.

questions.prompt: The process that makes fresh bread soft is called gelatinisation.
questions.promptGu: તાજી બ્રેડને નરમ બનાવતી પ્રક્રિયાને જેલેટિનાઇઝેશન કહે છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'This process, known as gelatinisation, gives fresh bread its soft and springy texture.' 'Known as' = 'is called'. So TRUE.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 2 માં લખ્યું છે કે 'gelatinisation' નામની પ્રક્રિયા તાજી બ્રેડને નરમ પોત આપે છે. 'known as' નો અર્થ 'called' જ છે. તેથી TRUE.

questions.prompt: The crust of old bread often becomes harder than the crust of fresh bread.
questions.promptGu: જૂની બ્રેડનો પોપડો ઘણી વાર તાજી બ્રેડના પોપડા કરતાં વધુ કડક બની જાય છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'the crust of an old loaf often feels soft and leathery rather than crisp'. The old crust becomes softer, not harder, so FALSE.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 3 મુજબ જૂની બ્રેડનો પોપડો કડક નહીં પણ નરમ અને ચામડા જેવો ('soft and leathery') લાગે છે. પ્રશ્ન 'વધુ કડક' કહે છે, તેથી FALSE.

questions.prompt: Bread kept in the refrigerator goes stale faster than bread kept at room temperature.
questions.promptGu: ફ્રિજમાં રાખેલી બ્રેડ ઓરડાના તાપમાને રાખેલી બ્રેડ કરતાં વધુ ઝડપથી વાસી થાય છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: starch chains rejoin 'up to three times faster than at room temperature, so bread kept in the fridge goes stale much more quickly'. 'Much more quickly' = 'faster'. TRUE.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 4 માં લખ્યું છે કે ફ્રિજમાં રાખેલી બ્રેડ 'much more quickly' એટલે કે ઘણી ઝડપથી વાસી થાય છે. તેથી TRUE.

questions.prompt: Most bakers freeze their own bread at the end of each day.
questions.promptGu: મોટા ભાગના બેકરો દરરોજના અંતે પોતાની બ્રેડ ફ્રીઝ કરે છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says bakers 'recommend' freezing bread that will not be eaten within two days. It gives their advice to others, but says nothing about what bakers do with their own bread each day. So NOT GIVEN.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 4 માં બેકરો બીજાને સલાહ ('recommend') આપે છે તે લખ્યું છે, પણ બેકરો પોતે દરરોજ શું કરે છે તે વિશે કંઈ લખ્યું નથી. તેથી NOT GIVEN.

questions.prompt: What happens during retrogradation?
questions.promptGu: રેટ્રોગ્રેડેશન દરમિયાન શું થાય છે?
options: Water enters the starch grains and the chains spread out.
The starch chains move back together and push water out of the grains.
The bread loses all of its water to the air.
Sugar in the bread turns into starch.
questions.answer: The starch chains move back together and push water out of the grains.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the chains 'start to move back together. They form a tight, ordered structure again and push water out of the grains. This change is called retrogradation.' Option A describes gelatinisation (paragraph 2), not retrogradation.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 3 મુજબ સ્ટાર્ચની સાંકળો ફરીથી નજીક આવે છે અને દાણામાંથી પાણી બહાર ધકેલે છે; આને જ retrogradation કહે છે. પહેલો વિકલ્પ તો gelatinisation (ફકરા 2) નું વર્ણન છે, તેથી તે ખોટો છે.

questions.prompt: Why does freezing stop bread from going stale?
questions.promptGu: ફ્રીઝ કરવાથી બ્રેડ વાસી થતી કેમ અટકી જાય છે?
options: Because the cold kills the bacteria in the bread.
Because the water turns to ice and the starch chains cannot move.
Because the crust becomes crisp again.
Because freezing adds fat to the bread.
questions.answer: Because the water turns to ice and the starch chains cannot move.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: freezing stops the process 'because the water inside the bread turns to ice and the chains can no longer move'. 'Can no longer move' = 'cannot move'.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 4 માં કારણ આપ્યું છે: બ્રેડની અંદરનું પાણી બરફ બની જાય છે અને સાંકળો હલી શકતી નથી ('can no longer move'). બેક્ટેરિયા વિશે ફકરામાં કંઈ નથી.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, bread that has been reheated should be
questions.promptGu: લેખક મુજબ ફરી ગરમ કરેલી બ્રેડ ...
options: kept in a closed bag for two days.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5: 'Once the bread cools down, it goes stale even faster than before, so reheated bread should be eaten immediately.'
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 5 માં લખ્યું છે કે ઠંડી થયા પછી ફરી ગરમ કરેલી બ્રેડ પહેલાં કરતાં પણ ઝડપથી વાસી થાય છે, તેથી તેને તરત ('immediately') ખાઈ લેવી જોઈએ.

questions.prompt: Why do large loaves go stale more slowly than small rolls?
questions.promptGu: મોટી બ્રેડ નાના રોલ કરતાં ધીમે વાસી કેમ થાય છે?
options: They are baked at a higher temperature.
They have less surface compared with their size.
They are usually kept in the freezer.
questions.answer: They have less surface compared with their size.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6: large loaves stale more slowly 'since they have less surface compared with their size'. 'Since' gives the reason.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 6 માં 'since' શબ્દ પછી કારણ આપ્યું છે: મોટી બ્રેડનું કદની સરખામણીમાં બહારનું સપાટી-ક્ષેત્ર ઓછું હોય છે.

questions.prompt: Starch is made of long chains of sugar molecules packed tightly together in tiny ____ .
questions.promptGu: સ્ટાર્ચ ખાંડના અણુઓની લાંબી સાંકળોથી બનેલો છે, જે નાના-નાના ____ માં ગાઢ રીતે ભરેલી હોય છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'long chains of sugar molecules that are packed tightly together in tiny grains'. The word after 'tiny' is 'grains'.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 2 માં બરાબર આ જ વાક્ય છે: 'packed tightly together in tiny grains'. તેથી જવાબ 'grains' (દાણા).

questions.prompt: Stale bread becomes soft again if it is heated to about 60 degrees ____ or higher.
questions.promptGu: વાસી બ્રેડને લગભગ 60 ડિગ્રી ____ કે તેથી વધુ ગરમ કરવાથી તે ફરી નરમ બને છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5: 'heated in an oven to around 60 degrees Celsius or higher'. 'Around' = 'about'.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 5 માં 'around 60 degrees Celsius' લખ્યું છે. 'around' અને 'about' બંનેનો અર્થ 'લગભગ' છે. જવાબ 'Celsius'.

questions.prompt: Bread made with fat, for example butter or ____ , stays soft for longer.
questions.promptGu: ચરબીવાળી બ્રેડ, જેમ કે માખણ કે ____ વાળી, વધુ સમય નરમ રહે છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 6: 'Bread made with fat, such as butter or oil, tends to stay soft for more days'. 'Such as' = 'for example'.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 6 માં 'such as butter or oil' લખ્યું છે. 'such as' એટલે 'for example' (જેમ કે). જવાબ 'oil' (તેલ).

questions.prompt: Bread that will be eaten soon should be kept at room temperature in a closed ____ .
questions.promptGu: જલદી ખાવાની હોય તે બ્રેડને ઓરડાના તાપમાને બંધ ____ માં રાખવી જોઈએ.
questions.explanation: Last paragraph: 'keep bread at room temperature in a closed bag if it will be eaten soon'.
questions.explanationGu: છેલ્લા ફકરામાં સલાહ છે: 'keep bread at room temperature in a closed bag'. જવાબ 'bag' (થેલી).

tests.title: Practice Test 2: Cities and Environment
tests.passage:
A Walk through the centre of almost any large city and you will see a landscape of flat grey roofs. For most of the twentieth century, these spaces were ignored and used only for air-conditioning units and water tanks. In recent decades, however, a growing number of city planners have begun to see rooftops as valuable land. One of the most popular ideas is the green roof: a roof that is partly or completely covered with plants growing in a layer of soil.

B The idea itself is not new. In northern Europe, especially in Scandinavia, people have covered their houses with turf for hundreds of years. The thick layer of grass and soil kept homes warm during the long winters and protected the wooden roof below from rain. Modern green roofs are far more technical, with special waterproof sheets and drainage layers to carry away extra water, but they rely on the same basic principle: a living surface can protect the building beneath it.

C One of the main benefits of green roofs is their effect on temperature. In summer, dark roofs absorb heat from the sun and can become hotter than 70 degrees Celsius. This contributes to what is known as the urban heat island effect, in which cities are several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. Plants, by contrast, use the sun's energy to evaporate water from their leaves, and this cools the air around them. Studies in several cities have found that the surface of a green roof can be up to 40 degrees cooler than a conventional roof on a hot day. As a result, the rooms below need less air conditioning, and energy bills fall. The plants also trap dust from the air, which makes city air slightly cleaner. In addition, a well-planted roof can attract bees, butterflies and small birds, even many floors above the busy streets.

D Green roofs also help cities to manage rainwater. When heavy rain falls on hard surfaces such as roads and ordinary roofs, the water runs off quickly into the drains. In many older cities, the drains can become overloaded, and dirty water may then overflow into rivers. A green roof acts like a sponge: the soil and plants hold a large part of the rain and release it slowly over several hours. Depending on the depth of the soil, a green roof can retain between 50 and 90 percent of the rain that falls on it in summer. This reduces pressure on the drains at exactly the moment when they are most at risk.

E Despite these advantages, green roofs are not suitable for every building. Wet soil is heavy, and many older roofs were not designed to carry such a load. Before a green roof is installed, engineers must check that the structure is strong enough, and sometimes expensive reinforcement is required. Installation costs are higher than for a standard roof, and the plants need regular care, especially in their first two years, when they are still becoming established. Leaks are rare when the roof is built properly, but if one does occur, finding it beneath the soil can be difficult and costly.

F Some governments have decided that the public benefits are large enough to justify official support. In certain cities, new commercial buildings with flat roofs must now include green areas, while other cities offer grants that cover part of the cost for home owners. Supporters argue that, as cities grow and summers become hotter, green roofs will change from an unusual feature into a normal part of urban design. Critics reply that the money might be better spent on planting trees at street level, where far more people can enjoy them. Whatever the outcome of this debate, it is clear that the roofs above our heads are no longer being ignored.

vocabulary.exampleGu: આખું દૃશ્ય લીલી ટેકરીઓથી ભરેલું હતું.

vocabulary.meaningEn: grass together with the soil its roots grow in
vocabulary.example: They laid new turf in the garden.
vocabulary.exampleGu: તેમણે બગીચામાં ઘાસવાળી માટીનો નવો થર પાથર્યો.

vocabulary.meaningEn: a system for carrying away extra water
vocabulary.example: Good drainage stops the field from flooding.
vocabulary.exampleGu: સારો પાણીનો નિકાલ ખેતરમાં પૂર આવતું અટકાવે છે.

vocabulary.meaningEn: to take in heat, liquid or energy

vocabulary.exampleGu: કાળાં કપડાં વધુ ગરમી શોષે છે.

vocabulary.meaningGu: બાષ્પીભવન થવું, વરાળ બનીને ઊડી જવું
vocabulary.meaningEn: to change from liquid into gas
vocabulary.example: Water evaporates quickly in hot weather.
vocabulary.exampleGu: ગરમ હવામાનમાં પાણી ઝડપથી વરાળ બનીને ઊડી જાય છે.

vocabulary.meaningEn: ordinary; of the usual type

vocabulary.exampleGu: ઇલેક્ટ્રિક ગાડીઓ સામાન્ય ગાડીઓ કરતાં ઓછો અવાજ કરે છે.

vocabulary.meaningEn: making a structure stronger by adding material

tests.title: Practice Test 3: Psychology
tests.passage:
Few experiences are as widely disliked as boredom. Children complain about it on long journeys, office workers try to escape it by checking their phones, and entire industries now exist to make sure that nobody ever has to spend a moment without entertainment. Yet a growing body of psychological research suggests that boredom may be less of an enemy than we assume. In my view, our determination to eliminate it entirely may be doing us more harm than good.

It is worth being clear about what boredom actually is. Psychologists generally describe it as an unpleasant state in which a person wants to be engaged in a satisfying activity but cannot find one. It is not the same as relaxation, which is pleasant, nor is it the same as apathy, in which a person has no desire to do anything at all. Boredom, in other words, contains a hidden message: it tells us that our current situation is not meeting our needs and that we should look for something better.

Seen in this way, boredom has a useful function. Researchers have argued that, like hunger or pain, it acts as a signal that pushes us towards change. A person who is bored at work may start looking for a more challenging position; a student who is bored by a textbook may search for a more interesting way to learn the same material. Without this uncomfortable feeling, we might happily remain in situations that are not good for us.

There is also evidence that boredom can encourage creativity. In one frequently cited experiment, a group of participants was first asked to complete a dull task: copying numbers from a telephone directory for fifteen minutes. They were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with a group that had not done the boring task, they produced more ideas, and their ideas were judged to be more original. The researchers suggested that when the mind is under-stimulated, it begins to wander, and this daydreaming allows unusual connections to form. Although a single study cannot prove a general rule, similar results have been reported by other teams, and I find the pattern convincing.

The difficulty is that modern technology has made boredom remarkably easy to avoid. A smartphone offers an endless supply of messages, videos and games, and many people reach for it the moment they feel even slightly under-occupied. Surveys suggest that adults in many countries check their phones dozens of times each day, often without any clear purpose. Each time we do this, we remove the discomfort that might have led to reflection or to a new idea. It would be an exaggeration to blame technology for every decline in creative thinking, but I believe it has quietly taken away an experience that once came to us naturally.

None of this means that all boredom is good. Chronic boredom, which continues for long periods, has been linked to poor mental health, overeating and risky behaviour, particularly among teenagers. People in repetitive jobs with no possibility of change may suffer real harm from it. The point is not that we should seek out boredom for its own sake, but that short periods of it, followed by a search for something meaningful, are a normal and healthy part of life.

What, then, should we do? Some educators recommend that parents resist the urge to fill every free moment of their children's time with organised activities. A child left alone on a rainy afternoon may complain at first, but is often the one who invents a game, builds something or starts writing a story. Adults, too, could benefit from small changes, such as leaving the phone in another room during a walk or a train journey. These suggestions may sound trivial, but they could restore a space in which our minds are free to wander. Boredom, after all, is not a problem that technology needs to solve; it is a message that we should learn to listen to.

tests.title: Practice Test 4: Animal Behaviour
tests.passage:
A Each spring, a strong colony of honeybees may do something remarkable: it divides itself in two. The old queen leaves the hive with roughly two-thirds of the workers, often around ten thousand bees, while a newly reared queen stays behind with the rest. The departing group, known as a swarm, flies only a short distance before settling on a tree branch, where it hangs as a dense cluster. It is here, often in full view of passers-by, that the bees must solve one of the most important problems of their lives: where to build their new home. They cannot delay for long, because the swarm carries only the honey stored in the bees' own bodies, which will last for just a few days.

B The choice matters enormously. A colony that selects a poor site may not survive the following winter. Through careful observation and experiments with artificial nest boxes, biologists have established what honeybees look for. The preferred cavity has a volume of about forty litres, large enough to store sufficient honey for the winter but not so large that it is difficult to keep warm. The entrance should be small, located near the bottom of the cavity, and positioned several metres above the ground, where it is easier to defend against predators. Remarkably, when researchers offered swarms a choice of boxes, the bees almost always chose the one that met these conditions best.

C Surprisingly, the queen plays no part in the decision. Instead, the task falls to a few hundred of the oldest and most experienced workers, called scouts. These bees fly out from the cluster and search the surrounding countryside, sometimes several kilometres away, for hollow trees, holes in walls and other possible nest sites. A scout that finds a promising cavity inspects it carefully, walking around the inside for up to forty minutes, apparently in order to judge its size. Meanwhile, the great majority of the swarm remains quietly in the cluster, saving energy and protecting the queen at its centre.

D When a scout returns to the swarm, she reports her discovery by performing a waggle dance on the surface of the cluster. The angle of the dance indicates the direction of the site in relation to the sun, while the length of the waggle shows its distance. Crucially, the number of times a scout repeats her dance depends on the quality of the site: a scout that has found an excellent cavity may dance more than a hundred circuits, whereas one that has found a mediocre site may perform only a few. Other scouts that watch the dance may then fly out to inspect the site themselves and, if they approve of it, return to dance for it too.

E This system produces a kind of competition between sites. At first, scouts may advertise a dozen or more locations. Because the best sites attract longer and more enthusiastic dances, they recruit more new visitors, while support for weaker sites gradually fades as their scouts stop dancing. Researchers have also discovered that scouts supporting one site sometimes deliver a brief head-butt, accompanied by a beeping sound, to scouts dancing for a rival site. This so-called stop signal appears to speed up the process by discouraging support for competing options.

F The final decision is not made by counting dances on the swarm. Instead, it occurs at the nest site itself. When scouts at a cavity sense that around twenty or thirty of their fellow scouts are present at the same time, they appear to conclude that agreement has been reached. This threshold is known as a quorum. The scouts then return to the cluster and produce a high-pitched piping sound, which signals to the other bees that they should warm up their flight muscles. About an hour later, the entire swarm takes off and flies, guided by the scouts, to its new home. The whole process typically takes between several hours and a couple of days.

G Scientists believe that the honeybee method offers lessons for human groups. The swarm makes good choices because it combines independent investigation, open competition between ideas and a decision rule that requires a significant level of agreement without waiting for everyone to agree. Some researchers have suggested that committees could benefit from similar principles, for example by encouraging members to examine options independently before any discussion and by limiting the influence of a single dominant leader. Whether such lessons can be fully applied to humans remains open to debate, but the bees' success suggests that a group can sometimes be wiser than any of its individual members. Perhaps the most striking feature of the system is that no single bee ever compares all the options; good decisions emerge from many simple interactions.

tests.title: Practice Test 5: Society and Policy
tests.passage:
It has become an article of faith in modern administration that what cannot be measured cannot be managed. Hospitals are ranked by waiting times, universities by the number of times their research is cited, schools by examination results and police forces by the number of crimes they record. The appeal of such figures is obvious: they promise transparency, allow comparison across institutions and appear to replace the vague impressions of insiders with hard evidence. Yet the enthusiasm for quantification has run considerably ahead of any serious reflection on its costs, and it is these costs, rather than the familiar benefits, that I wish to examine here.

The most fundamental difficulty is that a number is never a neutral description of the activity it purports to capture. To measure anything, one must first decide what counts, and that decision inevitably privileges some aspects of performance over others. A hospital assessed on the proportion of patients seen within four hours is being told, implicitly, that the speed of initial contact matters more than, say, the quality of the conversation between doctor and patient, which no one has found a convenient way to count. Over time, what is measured tends to be mistaken for what is valuable, and those features of good work that resist quantification are quietly neglected. This happens not because anyone has decided that they are unimportant, but because they have become invisible.

A second and more corrosive problem arises once figures are tied to rewards or penalties. An observation often associated with the economist Charles Goodhart holds that once a measure becomes a target, it loses much of its value as a measure. People are not passive objects of assessment; they are intelligent agents who respond to incentives, and they will rationally direct their efforts towards whatever is being counted. Thus a surgeon judged on survival rates may be tempted to decline the riskiest patients, a school judged on the share of pupils reaching a particular grade may concentrate its attention on those just below the grade boundary, and a police force under pressure to reduce crime may find ways of recording incidents as something less serious. In each case the figures improve while the underlying reality stays the same or even worsens.

Defenders of measurement are by no means naive about such distortions. Their usual response is that the remedy lies in better metrics: more indicators, more sophisticated adjustments for risk, more frequent audits. I am not persuaded. Each new indicator creates fresh opportunities for gaming, and each additional layer of audit consumes time that professionals might otherwise devote to the work itself. Doctors and teachers in many countries now report spending a substantial part of their week recording information for others to inspect, and it would be surprising if the quality of their actual work had not suffered as a result. The pursuit of a perfect metric, in short, risks becoming an endless cycle in which the cure reproduces the disease. Moreover, the more complex the system of indicators becomes, the harder it is for anyone outside the institution, including the public it is supposed to serve, to understand what the figures actually mean. Transparency, which was the original justification for measurement, is thereby gradually lost.

It would be equally mistaken, however, to conclude that measurement should be abandoned. Before figures were collected systematically, serious failures could remain hidden for years, protected by professional loyalty and the understandable reluctance of insiders to criticise their colleagues. Published data on matters such as infection rates or the outcomes of particular operations have undoubtedly exposed poor practice that would otherwise have continued. Numbers, in other words, can give a voice to patients, parents and citizens whom institutions might prefer to ignore. The real question is therefore not whether to measure, but how measurement ought to be used.

Here a distinction proposed by several researchers seems to me especially valuable: the distinction between measurement for learning and measurement for judgement. Indicators are at their most useful when they are collected by practitioners themselves, interpreted in context and used to diagnose problems that can then be discussed openly. They become most damaging when they are stripped of that context, published as simple league tables and linked directly to funding or careers. A falling score in the first setting is an invitation to ask why; in the second, it is a threat to be avoided by any available means. A sensible system would therefore keep quantitative indicators but combine them with qualitative inspection, conducted by experienced peers who can see what the figures leave out. Such inspection is slower and more expensive than reading a spreadsheet, but its judgements are far harder to manipulate.

Underlying the whole debate is a question of trust. The demand for ever more measurement typically reflects a suspicion that professionals cannot be relied upon to act in the public interest unless they are constantly watched. There is a painful irony in this, since a regime of continual surveillance tends to erode precisely the sense of professional responsibility it was meant to replace. Those who feel that only their numbers matter will, sooner or later, care only about their numbers. None of this implies that professionals should be beyond scrutiny. It suggests, rather, that we approach our figures with a degree of humility, remembering that they are tools for understanding a complex reality and not substitutes for it.

questions.prompt: The benefits of performance figures have received less attention than their costs.
questions.promptGu: કામગીરીના આંકડાના ફાયદાઓ પર તેમના ગેરફાયદા કરતાં ઓછું ધ્યાન અપાયું છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'the enthusiasm for quantification has run considerably ahead of any serious reflection on its costs', and the writer calls the benefits 'familiar'. So the writer thinks the costs, not the benefits, have been neglected. NO.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 1 મુજબ આંકડાઓ માટેનો ઉત્સાહ તેના ગેરફાયદા પરના વિચાર કરતાં ઘણો આગળ નીકળી ગયો છે, અને ફાયદા તો 'familiar' (જાણીતા) છે. એટલે લેખક માને છે કે ગેરફાયદા પર ઓછું ધ્યાન અપાયું છે – પ્રશ્નનું ઊલટું. તેથી NO.

questions.prompt: Aspects of work that are hard to count are neglected because managers have deliberately judged them unimportant.
questions.promptGu: ગણવામાં મુશ્કેલ હોય તેવાં કામનાં પાસાંની અવગણના થાય છે કારણ કે મેનેજરોએ જાણીજોઈને તેમને બિનમહત્ત્વનાં ગણ્યાં છે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: such features are neglected 'not because anyone has decided that they are unimportant, but because they have become invisible'. The writer rejects the reason given in the statement. NO.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 2 માં સ્પષ્ટ લખ્યું છે: કોઈએ તેમને બિનમહત્ત્વનાં ગણ્યાં હોવાથી નહીં, પણ તે દેખાતાં બંધ ('invisible') થઈ ગયાં હોવાથી અવગણના થાય છે. લેખક આ કારણ નકારે છે, તેથી NO.

questions.prompt: Introducing more indicators and audits is likely to solve the problem of gaming.
questions.promptGu: વધુ સૂચકાંકો અને ઓડિટ ઉમેરવાથી આંકડા સાથે રમત (gaming) ની સમસ્યા ઉકેલાઈ જશે.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: after describing the call for 'more indicators ... more frequent audits', the writer says 'I am not persuaded. Each new indicator creates fresh opportunities for gaming'. NO.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 4 માં વધુ સૂચકાંકો અને ઓડિટના ઉપાય પછી લેખક કહે છે 'I am not persuaded' (મને ખાતરી નથી) – દરેક નવો સૂચકાંક ગેમિંગની નવી તક ઊભી કરે છે. તેથી NO.

questions.prompt: Published data have revealed poor practice that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.
questions.promptGu: પ્રકાશિત આંકડાઓએ એવી ખરાબ કાર્યપદ્ધતિ ખુલ્લી પાડી છે જે અન્યથા ધ્યાનમાં ન આવત.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5: published data 'have undoubtedly exposed poor practice that would otherwise have continued'. 'Exposed' = 'revealed'; 'undoubtedly' shows the writer's agreement. YES.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 5 માં લેખક કહે છે કે પ્રકાશિત આંકડાએ 'undoubtedly' (નિઃશંકપણે) ખરાબ કાર્યપદ્ધતિ ખુલ્લી ('exposed' = revealed) પાડી છે. તેથી YES.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's purpose in the first paragraph?

To introduce a discussion of the drawbacks of relying on measurement.
To explain why insiders' impressions are more reliable than figures.
To describe the history of public administration.
questions.answer: To introduce a discussion of the drawbacks of relying on measurement.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 ends: 'it is these costs, rather than the familiar benefits, that I wish to examine here'. 'Costs' = 'drawbacks'. The paragraph sets up the topic of the passage.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 1 ના છેલ્લા વાક્યમાં લેખક કહે છે કે હું અહીં ગેરફાયદા ('costs' = drawbacks) તપાસવા માંગું છું. એટલે આ ફકરો આખી ચર્ચાની શરૂઆત (પરિચય) કરે છે.

options: To show that doctors are too busy to talk to patients.
To give an example of something valuable that is difficult to measure.
To suggest that waiting times are not important.
To criticise the training of hospital staff.
questions.answer: To give an example of something valuable that is difficult to measure.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: the conversation is something 'which no one has found a convenient way to count'. It illustrates the 'features of good work that resist quantification'.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 2 માં કહ્યું છે કે આ વાતચીતને ગણવાનો કોઈ સરળ રસ્તો નથી ('no one has found a convenient way to count'). એટલે તે એવી મૂલ્યવાન બાબતનું ઉદાહરણ છે જે માપી શકાતી નથી.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude towards the defenders of measurement in the fourth paragraph?
questions.promptGu: ચોથા ફકરામાં માપદંડના સમર્થકો પ્રત્યે લેખકનું વલણ કેવું છે?
options: He accepts that they recognise the problem but rejects their proposed solution.
He believes they are unaware of the distortions caused by targets.
He fully supports their call for better metrics.
He thinks they are mainly interested in saving money.
questions.answer: He accepts that they recognise the problem but rejects their proposed solution.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'Defenders of measurement are by no means naive about such distortions' (they recognise the problem), but about their remedy of 'better metrics' he says 'I am not persuaded' (he rejects it).
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 4 માં લેખક સ્વીકારે છે કે સમર્થકો ભોળા નથી – તેઓ સમસ્યા જાણે છે ('by no means naive'). પણ તેમના ઉપાય ('better metrics') વિશે લેખક કહે છે 'I am not persuaded' – એટલે ઉપાય નકારે છે.

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the writer's overall position?
questions.promptGu: કયું વિધાન લેખકના કુલ મતનો શ્રેષ્ઠ સાર આપે છે?
options: Measurement should be abolished because it destroys professional responsibility.
Measurement is useful mainly as a tool for learning, combined with qualitative judgement.
League tables are the best way to make professionals accountable.
Professionals should not be inspected by anyone outside their profession.
questions.answer: Measurement is useful mainly as a tool for learning, combined with qualitative judgement.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 rejects abandoning measurement ('It would be equally mistaken ... to conclude that measurement should be abandoned'). Paragraph 6 supports 'measurement for learning' and combining indicators 'with qualitative inspection'. The last paragraph says professionals should not be 'beyond scrutiny', so the final option is wrong.
questions.explanationGu: ફકરા 5 માં લેખક માપદંડ બંધ કરવાનું ખોટું ગણે છે. ફકરા 6 માં તેઓ 'measurement for learning' (શીખવા માટે માપન) અને ગુણાત્મક નિરીક્ષણ સાથે જોડવાનું સમર્થન કરે છે. છેલ્લા ફકરામાં લખ્યું છે કે વ્યાવસાયિકો તપાસથી પર નથી, એટલે છેલ્લો વિકલ્પ પણ ખોટો છે.
